title: Wear the Yoke and Live
overview: Jeremiah wears an ox yoke to warn Judah and its neighbors that rebelling against Babylon will ruin them, while accepting its rule will let them survive.

parts.label: A yoke for five kings (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: The standard Hebrew text dates this to King Jehoiakim, but a few manuscripts and early translations read Zedekiah, and most scholars prefer that, since the envoys come to Zedekiah (v. 3) and the next chapter places these events in his reign. Envoys from five nearby kingdoms had gathered in Jerusalem, likely to plan a revolt against Babylon, and Jeremiah puts on an ox yoke of straps and wooden bars and sends word that it pictures what awaits their kings.

parts.label: Power handed to Babylon (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: As maker of the earth, God claims the right to give power to anyone he chooses, and he even calls Babylon's conquering king his "servant," meaning the one he is using for now. That rule has a limit: Babylon itself would later fall, as it did to Persia in 539 BC.

parts.label: Bend or be broken (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Nations that resist will face war, hunger and disease, while those that accept Babylon's rule will stay on their land and farm it. The fortune tellers and dream readers promising freedom were, in Jeremiah's view, leading their people straight into exile.

parts.label: The same warning to Judah (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Jeremiah tells Zedekiah directly to submit and live, and says the prophets promising otherwise speak in God's name without being sent. Zedekiah later rebelled anyway, and Babylon destroyed Jerusalem around 587 BC.

parts.label: False hope about temple treasures (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: Babylon had already carried off many sacred objects from the temple in 597 BC, and some prophets said they would soon come back. Jeremiah answers that real prophets would instead pray that the things still left would not be taken too.

parts.label: Even what remains will go (vv. 19-22)
parts.note: The great bronze pillars, the huge bronze water basin called the Sea, and the wheeled stands would all be hauled to Babylon. Yet the chapter ends with a promise of return, and the book of Ezra describes temple objects being sent back under Persian rule.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether Jeremiah's call to submit to Babylon offers a lasting principle about accepting harsh or unjust rulers, or was a one-time word meant only for that crisis.
think: When the people around you are saying exactly what you hope to hear, how do you tell honest hope from comforting wishful thinking?
